blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
The following is a press release from the Social Security System.

The Social Security System (SSS) and the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on October 21 to expand social security protection for the country’s estimated 1.5 million freelancers and virtual assistants.
SSS President and Chief Executive Officer Victor Alfonso A. Limlingan and DICT Secretary Robert Joseph M. de Claro led the signing ceremony at the DICT office in Quezon City.

Limlingan said the MOU establishes a strategic partnership to strengthen the online freelancing industry through capability-building, competency development and expanded social security coverage for Filipino freelancers.

“A key objective of the MOU is to increase awareness, registration, membership and compliance with Republic Act No. 11199, or the Social Security Act of 2018, among freelancers and online workers, ensuring broader access to social security protection,” he said.
Limlingan emphasized the importance of extending social security protection to freelancers and virtual assistants, noting that they play an increasingly vital role in the country’s digital economy.

“Freelancers and virtual assistants are an important and growing segment of our workforce. By bringing them into the SSS coverage, we ensure that they, too, can access the same protection and benefits enjoyed by other workers—whether in times of sickness, maternity, disability, retirement, or even death,” Limlingan said.
He added that the partnership reflects the SSS’ commitment to leave no worker behind.

“Our goal is simple: no Filipino worker should be left without social security protection. Through this MOU with DICT, we are taking a significant step toward making social security more accessible, more relevant, and more responsive to the needs of our digital workforce,” Limlingan said.

Through the partnership, freelancers and virtual assistants will be encouraged to register as self-employed SSS members, making them eligible for benefits such as sickness, maternity, disability, retirement, funeral and death benefits.

As self-employed members, they may also apply for SSS loan programs, including salary loans, the Emergency Loan Program and the SSS Micro Loan Program. Members may likewise obtain additional coverage under the Employees’ Compensation (EC) Program for work-related sickness, disability or death.
The SSS contribution rate currently stands at 15%. For self-employed members, the Monthly Salary Credit used to determine contributions ranges from ₱5,000 to ₱35,000.
Limlingan said the lowest monthly contribution is ₱760, consisting of ₱750 for the regular SSS contribution and ₱10 for the Employees’ Compensation contribution.
“The highest monthly contribution is ₱5,280, composed of ₱3,000 for the regular SSS contribution, ₱30 for the EC contribution and ₱2,250 for the Mandatory Provident Fund,” he said.

Under the MOU, the SSS and DICT will also explore joint initiatives on freelancer education, partnerships, job creation and matching, advocacy activities and the monitoring of program outcomes to support the growth and sustainability of the freelancing ecosystem. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results
articles.summary: German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.

image.caption: No candidate in Israel has a clear path to powerImage: David Goldman/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Though it has been two days since Israel's parliamentary elections, German politicians are still being cautious to respond, as it is still unclear who will lead the new government. Although the right-wing bloc including religious hardliners led by incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is ahead of the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, neither has a clear path to a governing majority in the Knesset. Forming a coalition government is likely to be extremely difficult.

Martin Giese, spokesperson for German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, declined to comment at Wednesday's regular government press conference in Berlin. but he did stress that Germany has been in contact with numerous officials and politicians in Israel via Germany's ambassador. "The Jewish state and Germany are inextricably linked by our history, and we will do everything we can to work well with any future government," Wadephul said.
No clear winner emerges in Israel's election
Alabali Radovan: 'Winter in Gaza will be difficult'
One concern for the German government is providing aid to the people in Gaza, and protracted coalition negotiations could delay necessary progress.

"Winter is coming, and it will be difficult," Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan, currently visiting Lebanon, warned in an interview with Politico. She underlined that there must be more opportunities for aid organizations to provide crucial assistance in Gaza — and that it cannot wait for coalition negotiations.

In interviews with DW and broadcaster RTL, she spoke about the recent increase in attacks by Israeli settlers in the West Bank and east Jerusalem on Palestinian residents: "The radical settler violence must be stopped. The Netanyahu government remains in office on an interim basis, and this means that this situation must still be brought to an end." All settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territories is considered illegal under international law.
More distanced from Netanyahu's government

Relations between Germany and Israel have long been particularly close — in part due to Germany's historical responsibility for the murder of millions of European Jews during the Nazi era. Recently, however, the German government has distanced itself from Netanyahu's policies, at least in its public rhetoric.

Most recently, Wadephul said after a major Israeli military operation near the city of Hebron: "Under international law, Israel is quite clearly obligated to uphold and protect the rights of Palestinians as well." Around 3,000 Palestinians were driven from their homes during the operation, which followed the reported killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinians.

In Berlin, there has long been speculation about whether Germany's policy toward Israel might change after the election. So far, one thing is clear: Unlike numerous other countries, including some in Europe, Germany does not intend to recognize a Palestinian state for the time being.
Israeli army demolishes Palestinian buildings in Hebron
CDU hoping for a centrist government
At the same time, Germany hopes that the future government will no longer include religious extremist, and in some cases far-right, politicians such as the current Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

"I think it would be best for Israel to form a government that is closer to the center of the political spectrum," Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy expert for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in the Bundestag, told DW. "Of course, that's something the people — and above all, the elected politicians — will have to figure out. But it's encouraging that so many people participated in the election."

The Arab-majority parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel made big gains in this election. They are usually classified as part of the current opposition camp. Many analysts have noted that the historic results by these parties could lead them to play a kingmaker role in coalition formation.

However, Netanyahu’s bloc and various parties have ruled out working with the Arab-majority parties. Eisenkot's bloc has not stated whether it would be willing to form such a coalition, but one of the Arab-majority parties, United Arab List, featured a Jewish candidate, and has stated its willingness to work with Eisenkot’s bloc to unseat Netanyahu.

Hardt believes a minority government led by Eisenkot and supported by parties representing Arab Israelis is conceivable. "The major campaign carried out by Netanyahu's camp, aimed primarily against Arab Israelis, greatly mobilized the opposition, to the point where his camp no longer has a majority." The vice president of the German Bundestag, Green Party politician Omid Nouripour, told DW. "Frankly, after all the turmoil that has occurred — for example, regarding judicial reform — this is good news for Israeli democracy."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: What you need to know about the 2026 US midterm elections
articles.summary: Plenty is at stake in this midterm election as Democrats try to win majority control of the US Congress

items: Early voting for the November 3, 2026, midterm elections is underway, with over 100 million expected to vote and a record $3.8 billion spent on political ads, particularly in battleground Senate races.
Control of Congress is at stake, with Democrats needing to gain seats in both the House and Senate to take control, while midterm elections historically pose risks for the party in the White House.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, DC, USA – Early voting has been underway for weeks ahead of the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, when US voters will elect members of the House of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country.

Held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, the midterms by definition do not involve the president. But for anyone who thinks they lack drama or importance this year, consider these two statistics:

More than 100 million people likely will cast ballots in this year’s midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022; and as of October 12, a record $3.8 billion had been spent on political advertisements that have been aired so far. Top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio, and Michigan, according to AdImpact, which tracks the activities.
Elon Musk alone has spent about $366 million to support Republicans, according to campaign finance records.
Still, midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races. More than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election, for example.
Plenty is at stake in this midterm election as Democrats try to win majority control of the US Congress.

Currently, Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House, where there are two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to win control.

Democrats also are fighting to win the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. They must net four additional seats to get control. Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome.

Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress. For 2026, that means that President Donald Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.
The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president’s performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.
Midterm election results also can give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.
Approval of Trump’s performance is at an all-time low of 32%, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to have an impact on the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.
At the same time, there is evidence that Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans. If early voting trends continue, it could point to a Democratic win in November.
There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump’s immigration enforcement tactics.

However, a landslide for the Democrats is far from assured. Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism towards Democrats, a Republican spending advantage on campaigns, and fears from moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.
Recent history tells the story of the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.

In the 2010 midterms, during the Democratic presidency of Barack Obama, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama’s landmark healthcare reform legislation. Democrats lost their majority. In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.
The Republican wave was a “shellacking,” Obama lamented at the time. He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.
Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House. They gained a net total of 40 House seats, but lost a net two Senate seats.
This year’s elections also have races for governors in 36 of the 50 states and voting in nearly every state for seats in their state-level legislative bodies.
Currently, Republicans control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.

If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — second in line for the presidency after the vice president — is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York. He is currently the House Democratic leader.

Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to launch investigations into a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates. Jeffries repeatedly has said Democrats would look into what he has called “unprecedented levels of corruption” during the Trump administration.
Jeffries also would steer Democrats’ legislative priorities through the House. He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy, and other costs more affordable.

A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker’s gavel remains in that party’s hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job. Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump’s 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill.”

Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler’s bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign and an open seat in a Nebraska swing district where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran.
Also high on Democrats’ list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.
Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.

Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence. State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Russia: Critical newspaper 'Novaya Gazeta' to close
articles.summary: "Novaya Gazeta," one of the last remaining independent, critical media outlets in Russia, has announced it is closing under pressure from state authorities. Meanwhile, in Ukraine, evacuations have…

image.caption: In its editorial, the "Novaya Gazeta" wrote that its closure reflected the state of modern Russia under President Putin.Image: Dmitry Feoktistov/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced that it is shutting down and ceasing operations under pressure from state authorities who recently searched the home of its senior editor.
"They've killed us," read a statement published on the newspaper's website on Friday morning.

"The Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," added editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov in a video statement. "On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave."
What is the Novaya Gazeta?

Founded in 1993 following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Novaya Gazeta (Russian for "New Newspaper") was one of the few remaining critical media outlets in Russia, known for its investigations into corruption and its critical coverage of Russian politics.

It has always operated under pressure from state authorities but circumstances have deteriorated dramatically since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with the Kremlin introducing near-Soviet levels of media censorship.

The vast majority of independent journalists have been forced into exile and those who have remained in Russia have been designated "foreign agents" — a label which imposes a wide range of restrictions in everyday life including on the right to earn income from rent, interest payments or royalties from intellectual work.

A former Novaya Gazeta editor-in-chief, ​Dmitry Muratov, dedicated his 2021 Nobel Peace ​Prize to six colleagues who were killed because ​of their work — including Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by the Russian military in Chechnya and was found dead in her apartment block on President Vladimir Putin's birthday in October 2006.

"More than 30 years of life together with our country and its citizens will now end on the street," wrote the newspaper in its editorial, "without a basis for existence and under constant threat of repression."

The announcement of the outlet's closure comes two weeks after veteran editor-in-chief Sokolov was questioned by investigators in Moscow over "unlawful use of personal data" in connection with a criminal case against a colleague, Oleg Roldugin.

Roldugin had been detained and charged with obtaining "unlawful access to computerized information," an offence that carries a prison term of up to 10 years. No further details were given and Roldugin has pleaded not guilty.
International media rights groups have slammed the targeting of the Novaya Gazeta, with Reporters Without Borders calling on the Kremlin to "put an end to the judicial harassment" of its journalists.
Novaya Gazeta: 'The story of a country and a society being finished off'
In its editorial, the Novaya Gazeta wrote that its closure reflected the state of modern Russia under President Putin.
"This isn't just our personal story; it's the story of a country and a society that are being finished off in exactly the same way," it wrote.

"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated and their protection has been equated with a crime. Elections and elected bodies have been de facto eliminated. Public institutions have been dismantled. Freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled. Private life has been turned inside out by dirty hands.

"The courts have been destroyed, along with the law and the rule of law. Holding one's own convictions is now treason. But treason is when a state betrays its own Constitution. And this treason is an ongoing crime, currently unfolding before the eyes of the entire world."
Oleshky ceasefire comes into effect in Ukraine war
Oleshky: evacuations begin amid localized truce
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, the evacuation of stranded residents from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky began on Friday as a localized US-brokered ceasefire continued to hold into a fourth day.

Captured by Russian troops early in the war in 2022, locals had endured food, water and medicine shortages for months, with some being forced to hunt and eat pigeons, residents told the AFP news agency.
The population of Oleshky has since dropped from 24,000 to about 2,000, many of whom were on Friday set to be evacuated either to Russian-controlled or Ukrainian-controlled territory.

"Evacuation and distribution of humanitarian aid have begun," said Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia while Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova posted a video showing groups of people waiting to board buses.
The local ceasefire— announced by US First Lady Melania Trump last week — is the longest pause in fighting anywhere in Ukraine since the 2022 invasion. It is due to end on Sunday evening.

image.caption: In this May 2021 file photo, Russian men's hockey team players react during an IIHF men's hockey world championships match. A ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport on Friday has overturned an IIHF ban on Russian teams from its world championships instituted since the invasion of Ukraine in 20

blocks.text: Hockey·Breaking
Russia teams must be allowed to play International Ice Hockey Federation events such as the world championships, the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled on Friday.
Russia had been banned from competitions since 2022 following invasion of Ukraine
CAS overturned IIHF decisions which excluded Russia from events in the 2026-27 season including the men's and women's world championships.
In a brief statement, CAS cited a lack of sufficient evidence to support the IIHF's security concerns.

CAS said its ruling did not address issues such as whether Russia should be required to play without national symbols as a team of neutral athletes, as in some other Olympic sports, or other "organizational consequences."

items: IIHF to decide Russian hockey participation on event-by-event basis after ban review
Russia, Belarus remain banned from hockey tournaments until at least May 2026

blocks.text: The IIHF expressed disappointment with the ruling and said it "maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions."
"While the IIHF respects the authority of CAS and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments."
Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov wrote on the Telegram social media app that CAS "recognized the demands of the Russian Hockey Federation on key points as justified."
The IIHF has barred Russian teams from its world championships since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia also missed the Olympic hockey tournaments this year.
The ruling is an immediate challenge for new IIHF President Franz Reindl, whose home country of Germany hosts the men's world championship next year.

articles.title: Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities
articles.summary:
Forums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say experts

Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is…

blocks.text: Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.

In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.

Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.

The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.

Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.

Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.

“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.

In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.

Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

articles.title: Brazil's new anti-gang law: Can it curb organized crime?
articles.summary: A tough stance against organized crime? One year after a massacre that left more than 130 people dead, a new law aims to crack down on drug cartels in Rio's favelas.

image.caption: Residents of the "Complexa da Penha" favela in Rio watch in shock as bodies laid out in the street are being removed. More than 130 people were killed during the police operation on October 28, 2025Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: One year after the deadliest police operation in the history of Brazil, human rights organization Human Rights Watch (HRW) has leveled serious accusations against the country's authorities.
Contrary to legal regulations, most of the 2,500 police officers who were deployed to the "Complexo do Alemao" and "Complexo da Penha" favelas on October 28, 2025, did not wear body cameras.
In the course of "Operacao Contencao" ("Operation Containment"), police officers were expected to execute dozens of arrest warrants against members of the Comando Vermelho drug cartel that day.
The result: During hours-long firefights in the favelas, 117 alleged gang members and five police officers were killed.
Brazil election: Voters in Rio split over crime and policing
Body cameras don't show the full picture

After analyzing more than 4,000 hours of video material, HRW concluded in its investigation that only around one quarter of the deployed police officers were wearing body cameras and that some were manipulated. Not a single deadly shooting was captured on camera.
"It's clear to us that a decision by the Supreme Court according to which the police in Rio must wear body cameras was violated," said HRW Brazil director Cesar Munoz.
The organization published its report in Rio de Janeiro on October 28.
Having analyzed the autopsy findings, HRW also concludes that many bodies show signs of execution, i.e. the killing of persons already incapable of fighting.

blocks.caption: Excessive police violence: According to HRW, 40% of those killed were shot in the head and 75% were shot in the backImage: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: For example, 40% of those killed were shot in the head, and 75% were shot in the back. There were reasons to believe, Munoz said, that the operation "was obviously designed to be lethal."
The police operation carried out under the supervision of the state government of Rio de Janeiro shocked the country. However, there were soon calls to intensify the fight against organized crime.
Fighting drug gangs and militias

In response, the "Anti-gang Law" ("Lei Antifaccao") came into force in March 2026. It is aimed at combating criminal gangs like the PCC, a drug gang based in Sao Paulo, or the Comando Vermelho (CV), which dominates Rio.

However, militias (gangs made up of corrupt police officers and soldiers) are also to be dismantled, both criminally and economically. "The law addresses a real problem," Rodrigo Ghiringhelli de Azevedo of the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety (FBSP) NGO told DW.
This was because the ability of criminal organizations to control territories, move funds and make inroads into economic activities and public institutions had expanded.

blocks.caption: Police and military operations in Rio's favelas occur time and again. The "Anti-Gang Law" of March 2026 expands the police's powers in the fight against drug gangsImage: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: It was positive, he added, that the law extends tools for asset tracing, finance tracking, institutional cooperation and capital withdrawal to these organizations.

Another improvement, said HRW Brazil's Cesar Munoz, was closer cooperation between state security agencies. The federal police, which reports to the central government, was to play a greater role in combating gangs in the future.

In Brazil, military and civil police report to state governments. During the deadly operations in Rio de Janeiro's favelas, one year ago, command was under the authority of the state government of Rio de Janeiro — and, consequently, under the influence of local politics.
Overcrowded prisons and recruitment behind bars
On the other hand, however, the law was raising constitutional concerns, said the FBSP's Azevedo. For example, it provides for the automatic imposition of pretrial detention on suspects.

blocks.caption: Residents of a favela in Rio protest against police violence during operations targeting drug dealers in their neighborhoodImage: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Other plans included expansion of grounds for arrest, restrictions on the easing of prison conditions — such as furloughs and the suspension of the remainder of a sentence — as well as an extension of the length of stay in prisons.
This could further exacerbate Brazil's chronic prison overcrowding. "Brazil already has one of the largest prison populations worldwide, and the law could accelerate its growth," said Azevedo.
In addition, prison overcrowding in Brazil had the perverse side effect of allowing crime syndicates such as the PCC and Comando Vermelho to recruit new members there.
"Overcrowded prisons without adequate government control facilitate recruitment and strengthening of the very criminal factions that legislation intend to combat," Azevedo concluded.
"It would be important to prevent gangs from recruiting young people and to show those who've committed crimes new prospects in life," HRW's Cesar Munoz told DW.

blocks.caption: Brazil has one of the largest prison populations in the worldImage: Jonne Roriz/dpa/picture-alliance

blocks.text: Rodrigo Ghiringhelli de Azevedo of FBSP also sees a constitutional problem in the cancellation of prison assistance — a benefit that the state paid to the prisoners' dependents.

"Its cancellation means economic punishment for those who haven't committed any crime at all, including children. This runs afoul of the constitutional principle according to which punishments must not extend beyond the convicted person," Azevedo said.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Families in the US are opting for earlier measles vaccinations amid outbreak
articles.summary:
Parents are opting for a second shot of MMR vaccine sooner, which aligns with guidance in Germany, the UK and France

Measles cases are accelerating in the US, with twice as many confirmed…

blocks.text: Measles cases are accelerating in the US, with twice as many confirmed cases as last year, and more parents are opting for earlier vaccination – especially with the second dose of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, which can be given as soon as four weeks after the first.

Giving the second shot soon after the first aligns with what some other countries, such as Germany, the United Kingdom and France, recommend – and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) also says it’s an option.

“More parents have heard about doing it ‘early’,” said Elias Kass, a naturopathic physician and vaccine advocate in Seattle, Washington. The CDC typically recommends giving the first MMR shot after age one and the second between the ages of four and six. But Kass began recommending the MMRV shot, which combines the second MMR and chickenpox (varicella) into one, at 15 months of age when measles cases began increasing a few years ago.
More parents are taking that recommendation now, he said, adding that their thinking is pretty straightforward: “There’s no reason to wait, measles is here now.”
Margot Taylor, a mother in Chicago, has three young children with three different vaccination histories for the MMR vaccine.
“All three of them are fully vaccinated, but it’s had to be accelerated because of all of these increasing cases,” Taylor said. “We’ve gone backwards so much.”
Her oldest, born in 2019, received her shots at ages one and four. Measles “wasn’t on my radar”, Taylor said. “I wasn’t even thinking about it.”
But with her second child, born in 2023, Taylor was surprised when the pediatrician recommended the second shot at age two. Chicago was battling a measles outbreak, so they went ahead with it.
Her third child, born in 2025, received the first shot after her first birthday – and then the second shot only three months later, in June.

Taylor worried the shots might not work as well if they were so early. But evidence shows the vaccines still work well at earlier ages; the recommendation to give the MMR dose between four and six years is based more on logistical concerns, to ensure children have both shots before they enter kindergarten and to cut down on doctors’ visits because other shots are also typically given at those ages.

And Taylor knows how vital the MMR vaccines are. When her third daughter was too young to get the first dose, she was exposed to measles at an airport during the west Texas outbreak. When the baby, only a month old, developed a fever afterward, they rushed to the hospital and stayed in a negative-pressure room until the test was negative for measles.

“I am relieved, and I still cannot say enough how grateful I am” for the vaccines, Taylor said. But she still wonders at the need to make these decisions at all. “I never thought that I would have to be learning the vaccine schedules,” she said.

Germany had similar recommendations to the US until 2001, when an outbreak brought a wave of illness and death that led the country to recommend the first shot at 11 to 14 months and the second shot at 18 to 23 months. In 2020, they moved the second dose to four weeks after the first.

“There’s absolutely no indication so far that any kid that has been vaccinated twice in any rhythm would have a higher risk of measles than someone who’s been vaccinated according to the old rule,” said Catherina Becker, a scientist in Germany.

Her son was two and a half years old when he got his second measles vaccine – and that was delayed only because he was recovering from a case of chickenpox. The CDC should “absolutely” consider a stronger recommendation to give the second shot earlier, Becker said.

Some parents are also choosing to get their babies the first shot at the age of six months – which the CDC recommends in areas with outbreaks, before international travel, and after exposure to measles. Those infants should also receive a third dose.

If a mother was vaccinated against measles before a pregnancy, that immunity is shared in utero, so the baby is protected for the first few months of life. That’s why a third dose is recommended if infants receive the first dose early – because it’s possible the baby still has some maternal antibodies and thus doesn’t establish a strong response to a vaccine at six months.

The second MMR shot is different from other boosters. Most people mount a strong response to the first shot, which is why only one shot was recommended until 1989. But scientists discovered that some people don’t respond to the first shot and need a second – which is why the booster was recommended. That’s also why people born before 1989 may need to get a second shot now.
“It’s a second chance to respond for the first time,” Kass said.

Becker looks to past outbreaks to understand the effectiveness of the shots. In a 1998 outbreak in Alaska, only 17 people were sickened at a school where nearly all students – some 2,186 in total – had received measles shots. She compared it with a 2010 outbreak at a Waldorf school in Germany where nearly half of the 300 students were unvaccinated and 71 people were sickened.
“It shows you what the measles vaccine does for you – it protects you from getting this thing,” she said.

articles.title: Congressional Democrats send scathing letter to ICE and DHS decrying treatment of hunger strikers
articles.summary:
Immigrants at Texas detention facility, protesting harsh conditions, say they’ve been threatened with force-feeding

Members of Congress sent a scathing letter to federal immigration…

blocks.text: Members of Congress sent a scathing letter to federal immigration officials this week demanding answers about conditions inside a Texas immigration jail, as detained immigrants on a prolonged hunger strike claim officials are retaliating against them and threatening them with force-feeding.

A group of seven congressional Democrats sent the letter earlier this week to Markwayne Mullin, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) secretary, and David Venturella, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) acting director, protesting about the treatment of hunger strikers.

The El Valle detention facility in Raymondville, Texas, detaining men and women, has fallen under scrutiny in recent weeks for allegations of harsh conditions. Detained immigrants on hunger strike say the facility has substandard medical care, undrinkable water and guards that mistreat them. Some hunger strikers are also protesting against their prolonged detention and are asking for their cases to move more quickly or to be transferred closer to loved ones in other parts of the country.

“It is abundantly clear that DHS continues to demonstrate gross disregard for the health, dignity, personhood, and safety of our communities,” the group of lawmakers, led by the Illinois representative Delia Ramirez, said in their letter to the DHS and ICE. “However, we remain committed to conducting oversight, advocating for our constituents, and pursuing accountability.”
The representatives “unequivocally condemn” conditions reported at the facility.
“Whether they arose through indifference or inability, such conditions violate the … DHS and ... ICE documented detention standards,” the letter said.
“It’s clear that DHS continues to demonstrate gross disregard for our health, dignity, personhood, and the safety of our communities,” Ramirez posted on X.
The congressional letter comes as the number of people detained by ICE increases amid the Trump administration’s aggressive but quieter anti-immigrant crackdown.

In past weeks, senators from Georgia have similarly expressed concern about an ongoing hunger strike at the Folkston ICE detention center complex in their state. The Guardian reported last week that a man detained there died, even as allegations surfaced of force-feeding threats. The DHS denies the hunger strikers in Georgia have been threatened.
The latest letter, signed by Representatives Ramirez, Texas’s Greg Casar and Jasmine Crockett and others, also demands details about the detainee population, the quality of medical care and more.

“People should not be detained in these horrific detention centers – the hunger strikers should be released to their families and we demand that they receive protection from further detention and deportation,” the representatives wrote. “We also demand that you refrain from force-feeding any person in your custody.”

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said that the department responds to official correspondence through official channels and added that the representatives “should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from their districts – NOT vilifying law enforcement”.
The DHS did not provide proof that the detainees participating in the strike, whose relatives spoke with the Guardian, have any criminal history.

El Valle is owned by the Willacy County Local Government Corporation and operated by the private prison company Management and Training Corporation (MTC). The local government corporation did not respond to a request for comment. MTC referred all questions to ICE.
The Guardian spoke with three relatives of asylum seekers detained in El Valle, who have all been detained for nearly a year and are participating in the strike, which is approaching three weeks.

On 11 October, detained immigrants inside the El Valle facility launched the hunger strike. More than two dozen immigrants, from Russia, Cameroon and other countries, first participated, according to family members and advocates.
There are now four women and 10 to 20 men still participating in the strike, family members said.
One of the hunger strikers is Inna Eremeeva, an asylum seeker from Russia.

While in detention, “she started having serious pain in her legs and her hips”, Eremeeva’s husband, Alexei, said through an interpreter. “She feels a growth in her private areas. She has been declined any medical care to figure out what is going on.”

Alexei also said that officials earlier told hunger-striking women they would be transferred to another ICE facility to be force-fed. Other ICE detention centers in Texas have been used to force-feed detainees.
In a statement, an ICE spokesperson said that “allegations that detainees are being threatened are FALSE. No detainees are being force fed or threatened with force feeding.

“During hunger strikes, ICE continues to provide three meals a day, delivered to the detained alien’s room, and an adequate supply of drinking water or other beverages,” ICE added. “ICE is committed to ensuring the safety, security, and well-being of all individuals in its custody.”

Eremeeva arrived in the US in 2024 and requested asylum. In November 2025, during one of Eremeeva’s work trips as a truck driver, she was stopped at a border patrol checkpoint in Texas and arrested by officials. She has been in detention since.

The DHS said in a statement that Eremeeva entered the US “using the disastrous Biden administration CBP One app”, which was used to process asylum seekers and “released in the country completely unvetted”. Eremeeva remains in detention as she challenges ICE’s attempts to deport her.

“People are feeling hopeless and desperate in the black hole of ICE detention,” said Savannah Kumar, a staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Texas. “People in immigration detention centers across the country have had to resort to hunger strikes because they are caged in conditions that feel unsurvivable.”

Amaliia Gilmutdinova’s husband, Shokhrukh Abdullaev, is also detained and participating in the strike. Abdullaev also worked as a truck driver and was arrested in November 2025 at a checkpoint in Texas. He entered the country in September 2021 using the CBP One app, the DHS said.
“He is very afraid to say anything,” Gilmutdinova said about her husband through an interpreter. “He is very much afraid of being put back in isolation.”

Another man, whose daughter requested their names not be shared for fear of retaliation, is 63 years old and struggles with various health problems. He is participating in the hunger strike. The man calls his daughter frequently with panic attacks and she guides him through breathing exercises to calm him down, she said.

Kumar from the ACLU of Texas added that ICE “essentially locks people up away from their families indefinitely”, pointing to a recent fifth circuit court decision that ICE detainees in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi do not have the right to seek release on bond.
According to the 63-year-old man’s daughter, “the only thing he wants is to be able to see his family. He wants to be transferred.
“He is like a child, asking: ‘Why am I here? I didn’t do anything’,” she added.

articles.title: IIHF ordered to allow Russia back into world championships
articles.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has ruled that Russian teams must be allowed to take part in international ice hockey tournaments. The IIHF had banned Russia following the country's full-scale…

image.caption: Russian players last participated at the Olympics in Beijing just before the country's 2022 invasion of UkraineImage: Petr David Josek/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a statement published on Friday, the Court of Arbitration for Sport(CAS) said it had overturned International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) decisions, which exclude Russia from events during the 2026-27 season, including the men's and women's world championships.
In the statement, the CAS cited a lack of sufficient evidence to support security concerns cited by the IIHF in its decisions to exclude Russian teams from competition.

Specifically, it ordered the IIHF to allow Russia to participate in five upcoming tournaments, including the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany next May and the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship scheduled for November 2027 in Canada.

The first tournament affected by the ruling is the Men's World Junior Championship, which opens in Edmonton on December 26. The Women's World Championship being hosted by Denmark next Friday, November 6, is not mentioned in the statement.
Russia happy to be back, others less so

Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov hailed the CAS ruling, writing on the Telegram social media app that CAS had "recognized the demands of the Russian Hockey Federation on key points as justified."

The IIHF expressed disappointment with the ruling , saying it "maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions."
"While the IIHF respects the authority of CAS and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments."
Germany's ice hockey association, the DEB, also expressed disappointment at the decision.
"Our position is unchanged: We reject the return of Russian national teams to international ice hockey tournaments," DEB chairman Frank Lutz said.

The IIHF has barred Russian teams from its tournaments since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. This meant Russia also missed this year's prestigious Olympic hockey tournaments in Milan earlier this year.
Russia and its predecessor, the Soviet Union, are one of the most successful ice hockey-playing nations, having won 27 men's World Championships, second only to Canada (28).
Friday's ruling comes with the IIHF having just elected a new president – Germany's Franz Reindl took over from Luc Tardif of France earlier this month.

articles.title: ‘Swift justice’: Student List supporters focus on cleaning up Serbia’s rotten institutions
articles.summary:
After improbable election victory, the unconventional grassroots movement says it will prioritise dismissal of corrupt officials

In Belgrade’s Pioneers Park, just across from the national…

blocks.text: In Belgrade’s Pioneers Park, just across from the national assembly, a small crowd craned their necks to listen. One woman held aloft a placard reading “Love prevailed for the people and Serbia”. With a bouquet of media microphones in front of them, members of the Student List, the direct democracy movement that won an improbable but decisive victory in Sunday’s election, gathered under the trees.

Having spent days bathing in the euphoria of their unexpected triumph, the candidates’ focus was now clear: the cleaning up of the rotten institutions that had increasingly blighted the lives of Serbs over the 14 years of government by the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS). They called for the dismissal of many senior law enforcement officials, among them the chiefs of the criminal police, the paramilitary gendarmerie and an anti-terrorism unit.

blocks.caption: Student List supporters in Pioneers Park on Thursday, one with a placard saying ‘love prevailed for the people and Serbia’. Photograph: Guy de Launey/The Guardian

blocks.text: Student List candidate Svetlana Stanarević was applauded when she accused the officials of violating the law. She also called for the director of Serbia’s internal intelligence agency to resign, accusing him of running the organisation as “a party security service, not a state security service”.

There was approval, too, for the “reopening or expediting of cases” related to the disaster that sparked the student protest movement. Sunday will mark the second anniversary of the canopy collapse that killed 16 people at a renovated railway station in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. There have yet to be any convictions.
The announcements on Thursday were the Student List’s way of stressing they intended to put anti-corruption efforts at the heart of government.

“For years, for decades, people have been really frustrated,” said Iva Marković, a Student List candidate and political ecologist who founded the Right to Water initiative. “We see this as a time where everyone who was honestly and credibly working within [public] institutions can do their jobs. They are no longer under political pressure, and we ask them to do their jobs, which also means for prosecutors to prosecute, and police to investigate.”

blocks.caption: Iva Marković of Student List says prosecutors and police can now do their jobs properly. Photograph: Guy de Launey/The Guardian

blocks.text: Reinforcing the student movement’s key principles is also a way, perhaps, to allay concerns that the Student List might not know how to handle its stunning victory over Vučić and the SNS. The movement is not a traditional party. It does not have a hierarchy or leader – and although the students selected the list of candidates, they will not have any direct control over the people who have been elected, once they have been sworn in as MPs.
Marković said the common commitment the students and their parliamentary candidates had made should not be underestimated.

“The process didn’t start with the elections,” she noted, adding that preventing “individualism” from undermining core goals had been key to the student movement’s success. “When you dream together with some people, it’s very hard to forget this dream, even if you are in parliament.”

blocks.caption: Borko Stefanović says he does not want a second democratic coalition to fritter away its early promise.  Photograph: Guy de Launey/The Guardian

blocks.text: Borko Stefanović’s choice of a pizzeria themed around ’Allo ’Allo! as a meeting place reflects Serbia’s enthusiasm for British sitcoms of a certain vintage. Only Fools and Horses is a particular favourite, with its tales of thwarted schemes and broken dreams chiming strongly in a country that has been through turbulent times since the early 1990s.

Stefanović knows this better than most. He was part of the political movement opposed to Slobodan Milošević – and saw the democratic coalition that emerged from the overthrow of Serbia’s notorious former president fritter away its early promise. It is not a film he cares to watch a second time.

“There is this almost legendary saying in Serbia that we won on the 5th of October [2000] over Milošević, but we never had the 6th of October,” he said, adding that the Student List was correct to prioritise the dismissal of corrupt officials.

“Get the right people in the right places, bring swift legal justice, liberate institutions and the media, and allow the prosecutor’s office to arrest criminals. Everyone who wants to contribute to the reforms needs to get on board and to do everything we can to make this excellent example in Europe a lasting one.”

blocks.caption: Tara Blagojević thinks everything will be fine even if the election victors were a ‘political experiment’. Photograph: Guy de Launey/The Guardian

blocks.text: Perched on a sofa in a coffee roastery in Belgrade’s old town, Tara Blagojević was convinced the movement she has been a part of already had the right people in place. With the elections over, she said it was down to the successful candidates to form a government. The student assemblies will take a less active role, acting as “advisers or kind of supervisors”.

“Everything’s going to be fine,” Blagojević insisted, adding that although the Student List was “kind of a political experiment”, the people who will soon be sworn in as MPs “recognise each other’s strengths and are able to project who can be suitable to do certain things within the new government”.

Slobodan Tomić is optimistic about the Student List’s prospects. The Belgrade-born political scientist at the University of York has been following the student movement since its inception. “It is an extraordinary change,” he said of the party’s unconventional structure. “I couldn’t find any example across the world of anything similar happening.
“The MPs had to sign a pledge that they would follow through the programme that the Student List had created. So on paper, there isn’t much space for drift.”

The organisers of the famous Exit music festival are also convinced. They moved the event out of the country this year in protest at the policies of Vučić and the SNS. They confirmed that Exit would return to its home in Novi Sad next year.

The news further energised the crowd at Belgrade’s first big gig since the election, where the euphoria showed no sign of subsiding. Chants of “Victory!” welcomed Fontaines DC on stage among the shipping containers at the port of Belgrade. “Congratulations,” responded the Irish singer Grian Chatten. “This is your moment, not ours.”

A former punk rock bassist himself, Stefanović is sure that assessment is correct. “These wonderful, wonderful people from the Student List and the student movement, they know exactly what needs to be done,” he said. He added just one caveat from experience: “Don’t blow it.”

articles.title: Residents leave devastated Russian-occupied Oleshky as evacuation corridor opens
articles.summary: Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the frontline town, despite the lack of gas, electricity and running water.

blocks.text: The evacuation of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky is under way, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have confirmed.
A ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.

The residents of Oleshky who wish to leave have a four-hour window to do so. An evacuation convoy of 25 buses will allow up to 750 people to leave Oleshky until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
It is understood several hundred people have decided to stay in the town, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."
Ukrainian territory lies 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.
They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.
Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.

Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday. Lantratova later posted a video on social media from the town, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.

In videos posted by his own social media account, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."
Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.
An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."
Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind.
"The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise."
Her grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter.
"She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said.
"That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."

The ceasefire is due to be in force until the end of Sunday 1 November. It has provided the first few days of peace in the Kherson region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title: Helicopter carrying six people crashes in northern Indian state
articles.summary: The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.

blocks.text: A search for survivors is under way after a helicopter carrying six people, including five pilgrims, crashed in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand, officials say.

Uttarakhand's Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said the helicopter had crashed near a village close to Joshimath in Chamoli district. Rescue teams have been dispatched to the mountainous area, but the condition of those on board remains unclear.
The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.
The cause of the crash is also not yet known. The incident happened amid reports of heavy rain and poor visibility in the region.
Uttarakhand, a Himalayan state which borders China and Nepal, is home to some of Hinduism's holiest shrines and attracts millions of pilgrims every year.

Badrinath is one of four sacred sites on the Char Dham pilgrimage circuit, alongside Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri. Many devotees travel through steep Himalayan valleys to reach the temples, which are open for only part of the year because of harsh winter conditions.

articles.title: Severe rainfall and flood warnings issued for central Greece and western Turkey
articles.summary:
Turkey has seen powerful thunderstorms and a fatal tornado this week with more heavy rain expected

Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and…

blocks.text: Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.

Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85mph (140km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of more than 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.

blocks.caption: A satellite image shows Typhoon In-fa in the Pacific Ocean on Thursday.  Photograph: CSU/Cira & JMA/Jaxa/Reuters

blocks.text: Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150mph (240km/h), with winds gusting over 185mph (296km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

articles.title: [OPINION] From Super El Niño to the budget: What is the plan?
articles.summary: Why should citizens be forced to find the pieces of the puzzle instead of the government presenting the entire picture in the first place?

blocks.text: When mistakes have been made, we’re supposed to learn from them.
When it comes to transparency, however, many in the Bongbong Marcos administration seem to instead double down on avoiding transparency at a time when it is needed the most.
Case in point: the lack of a publicly accessible, updated Strategic El Niño Action Plan.

Hundreds of local government units have already declared a state of calamity. Agriculture and fisheries are already being affected. Our water security is at serious risk. Our health systems are already strained. And the peak of this Super El Niño has not even arrived yet.

Yes, it is understandable that this master plan needs to be flexible enough that some of its provisions could be reevaluated and even updated to improve responses to this pending crisis. Obviously, it also makes sense to have a division of labor across national agencies that would focus on responding to their covered sectors (i.e., agriculture, education, water, etc.).

Several agencies have already reported their strategies to deal with these impacts. For example, the Department of Agriculture proposed its P61.99-billion spending package for protecting food production and livelihoods. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources is monitoring the water situation across the country. Anticipatory action frameworks are being built to trigger responses before the peak.

But the lack of a publicly available and readily accessible overall Strategic El Niño Action Plan limits effective coordination among sectors and stakeholders in addressing these challenges. It prevents clear, efficient tracking of the quantity and effectiveness of expenditures, hindering the capacity to hold duty-bearers accountable.

Why should citizens be forced to find the pieces of the puzzle instead of the government presenting the entire picture in the first place? Why should we build our defenses against the Super El Niño without even knowing the overall blueprint?

Sadly, this is nowhere near the first time this administration has been shown lacking in its crisis communications. The same patterns emerge time and again: premature guarantees of readiness, inconsistent messaging, pronouncements of assistance without proper implementation, and centering much of its narrative on household-level responsibility.

This is not even the first time this year; remember how this government handled the energy crisis that is still ongoing these days? It is another reminder that our electricity bills could be increasing again soon because the peso is depreciating — that, and a bunch of factors, such as the government’s refusal to truly commit to transitioning away from fossil fuels.
It is more than fair to ask whose needs are really being addressed here. Speaking of needs…

No one should ever refuse to support bills that would mandate civil society and citizens’ participation in the national and local budgeting processes. After all, the budget that is intended for the Filipino people must be shaped by the Filipino people. It is a constitutional right of every citizen to be involved in decision-making processes, especially on an issue that involves their taxes, their well-being, and their future.

Yet there would not even be a need for this if there were a greener diet for public service instead of craving for pork — hard, soft, or however they like it figuratively cooked. There would be no need for this if there were no corruption in flood control projects or any other project.

No one in the government must ever be ignorant of the needs of the citizens they are sworn to serve. Yet the decisions made by the lower chamber of Congress in their version of the 2027 budget indicate they are not as aware of the needs of Filipinos as they should be.

Staying with the lens of the Super El Niño — projected to be the strongest in decades — reducing the budget for crop insurance, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund, or the entire health sector compared to their 2026 allotments just does not add up.

Aside from the procedural questions, there are other questions that must be asked: Do the allocations for constructing or rehabilitating water infrastructure projects go to communities that would be hit the earliest or the hardest by the pending droughts? Are these infrastructure projects designed to be truly resilient to current and future droughts, floods, and other hazards?

Public participation should never depend on who is in power. Transparency cannot depend on which lawmakers have thick enough skin for genuinely meaningful engagements. Accountability does not only apply after corruption has been exposed. Tears shed within air-conditioned hallways should not drown out the cries of the earth and the poor.

Whether it is the Super El Niño or any other issue, the public has the right and deserves to know not just how our money is being spent but also where, for what purpose, and for whom. We cannot expect citizens to trust duty-bearers who fail to answer these questions that are part of their mandate.
For anyone in public service, the best ability is accountability. For building a healthy democracy, the best currency is transparency. Never forget that. – Rappler.com
John Leo Algo is the national coordinator of Aksyon Klima Pilipinas.

articles.title: How drones and DNA testing are being used to hunt down invasive wild pigs in Manitoba
articles.summary: Thermal drones and environmental DNA testing are showing promise in strengthening Manitoba's fight against invasive, destructive and disease-carrying wild pigs.

image.caption: Squeal on Pigs says that with diligence and persistence, invasive wild pigs can be eradicated in Manitoba. (Ryan Brook/University of Saskatchewan)

blocks.text: Manitoba
Thermal drones and environmental DNA testing are showing promise in strengthening Manitoba's fight against invasive, destructive and disease-carrying wild pigs.
Experts warn animals pose risk of African swine flu spread if disease arrives in Canada

Squeal on Pigs, a public awareness campaign aiming to stop the spread of the invasive Eurasian wild boar and cross-bred pigs across the province, says eradication is within reach. It warns the invasive animal poses major risks, including spreading African swine fever, and wreaking havoc on agricultural land and ecosystems.
"We've got a real chance of being able to get rid of them, if we're persistent," said Wayne Lees, Squeal on Pigs program co-ordinator.
The program is organized by Manitoba Pork and gets funding from the federal and Manitoba governments.
The group logged 240 confirmed wild pigs spotted provincewide last year, as removal efforts increased.

Wild pig population control has been an ongoing issue since the 1980s, but Lees believes two key technologies — thermal imaging drones and environmental DNA testing of water samples — are pushing the province closer to being free of wild pigs.
He highlighted Alberta's rat control program as a proven model that shows years of sustained, targeted efforts can eradicate an invasive species from a province.
Wayne Lees, Squeal on Pigs program co-ordinator, says the program logged 240 confirmed wild pigs provincewide last year. (Chelsea Kemp/CBC)

Strides in technology are making it easier to track the pests. Thermal drones allow teams to survey dense and inaccessible terrain more easily, while DNA testing helps hone in on potential groups of the animals.
"We're making progress.… If we're diligent and maintain our efforts, we will be able to eradicate them from Manitoba," Lees said.
"Maybe in a decade we won't need to talk about this anymore."
Spruce Woods Provincial Park, about 140 kilometres west of Winnipeg, remains a major hot spot and a key target for eradication.
"It's an island of bush land surrounded by agriculture," Lees said. "The wild pigs can go in there and hide out, and then they've got a feed source."
African swine fever
The primary disease threat posed by the animals is African swine fever, which is highly contagious and fatal to both commercial and wild pigs, Lees said.
The disease, which poses no threat to humans, is currently not in Canada.
Lee warns that if the disease ever takes hold in wild populations, it could spread to commercial herds, devastating Manitoba's hog industry.
Manitoba developed a response plan to cull and dispose of hundreds of thousands of pigs if an outbreak should occur.

items: Researchers probe Prairie wetlands for signs of 'epidermal epidemic' in Manitoba frogs, salamanders
Alberta testing AI-powered drone technology in battle against wild boar

blocks.text: Cassidy Klima, executive director of Animal Health Canada, said Manitoba is leading the charge when it comes to eradicating the invasive species. The national organization brings together industry and governments to prepare for and manage foreign animal disease outbreaks.
If African swine fever spreads to Canada, wild pigs could severely jeopardize food security and pork production, Klima said.
Cassidy Klima, executive director of Animal Health Canada, is optimistic about getting rid of wild pigs. (Chelsea Kemp/CBC)
She pointed to recent outbreaks in Europe damaging pork industry exports as an example, including an outbreak in Finland that the Canadian Food Inspection Agency reported in August.
"If African swine fever gets into our commercial herds, it can really decimate our food, our pork sector," Klima said.
"If we don't safeguard against that, no one else will."

items: More stories from Southwestern Manitoba

blocks.text: The wild pigs originated from commercial wild boar farming in the 1980s. Klima said that in many cases, farms would shut down and release the animals into the wild.

Provincial regulation now prohibits wild boar farming to prevent further population expansion. A 2025 regulatory change under the Wildlife Act and the Exotic Wildlife Regulation banned importing or possessing the animals.
For now, Klima said she's optimistic for the future.
"Eradication is a true potential in Canada," she said. "We have a national strategy. We have a lot of people invested in seeing this through."
A group of wild pigs can leave a trail of destruction. (Submitted by Ryan Brook)
But declining population density presents challenges, making remaining groups of wild pigs harder to find, Klima said. That makes public awareness critical.

While the nocturnal wild pigs are rarely spotted directly, their environmental impact is stark, she said. A group of the animals, called a sounder, can leave trails of destruction across farms and pastures while devastating native ecosystems.
"They're not native to Canada.… they don't really fit into the environment," Klima said. "They just create a lot of damage."

items: Manitoba eyes plan to cull hundreds of thousands of pigs if African swine fever arrives
Prof says trapper's boar kill shows 'tsunami of wild pigs' is encroaching on northern Sask.

blocks.text: Eradication efforts focus on capturing and euthanizing entire groups to stop population growth, Lees said. Sounders usually include mature breeding females and their offspring.
Manitoba's harsh weather climate also helps slow reproduction rates compared with warmer southern regions such as Texas, he said.
Drones, DNA used in hunt for Manitoba's invasive wild pigs
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Chelsea Kemp is a multimedia journalist with CBC Manitoba. She is based in CBC's bureau in Brandon, covering stories focused on rural Manitoba. Share your story ideas, tips and feedback with chelsea.kemp@cbc.ca.

articles.title: MIAA vows turnover of CCTV to NNIC in November after Dizon rebuke
articles.summary: The Manila International Airport Authority (MIAA) on Friday promised to complete the turnover of the CCTV surveillance system to the Ninoy Aquino International Airport's (NAIA) private management by…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 5:32pm

The Manila International Airport Authority (MIAA) on Friday promised to complete the turnover of the CCTV surveillance system to the Ninoy Aquino International Airport's (NAIA) private management by November 2026.

This comes hours after Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon lashed out at airport officials for failing to turn over the security camera system to the New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC). Dizon gave the officials until November to complete the turnover before people start getting fired.

"MIAA has already completed the final acceptance of the CCTV project and initiated the necessary arrangements for its formal turnover to NNIC in accordance with the NAIA Public-Private Partnership Concession Agreement," the agency said in a statement.
"MIAA is committed to working closely with NNIC to resolve the outstanding matters and complete the turnover within the period directed by the Secretary," it added.
The MIAA explained that it already initiated the turnover and acceptance agreement. It is also continuing CCTV repair and restoration efforts.

Dizon was then appointed into the Department of Public Works and Highways, with Giovanni Lopez replacing him as Transport Secretary. Dizon and Lopez were switched Cabinet posts last Monday, with the former assuming his role as DOTr Secretary once more. — VDV, GMA News

Rappler

The Villars aren’t saying much about the possible mall sale, but their long-delayed financials hint at billions in debt repayments that could be pushing them to part with some of their prized possessions

items: The Villar group is facing heavy debt repayments, leading to the potential sale of retail properties.
Vista Mall Santa Rosa, which opened in 2015, is reportedly being marketed with an asking price of P8 billion.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
First was AllDay in Libis. Now, possibly, Vista Mall Santa Rosa. As the Villar group faces heavy debt repayments, it seems their once-prized retail locations appear to be up for grabs.

The former AllDay supermarket site along C-5 in Libis, Quezon City, is now with Robinsons Retail Holdings Incorporated, a source with the Gokongwei group confirmed to Rappler. Shopwise is expected to open there by December, just a few steps away from RRHI’s office.

But that might just have been the start. An industry source familiar with the Villars hinted that more properties across the family’s businesses could change hands, with Vista Mall Santa Rosa possibly the latest to be shopped around.

Opened in April 2015 along the Santa Rosa-Tagaytay Road near Nuvali, Vista Mall Santa Rosa is a sprawling commercial complex housing an AllHome store, supermarket, cinemas, restaurants, and office spaces for BPO tenants. The property has reportedly been advertised online with an P8-billion asking price.
Senior officials at a prominent property brokerage told Rappler they were aware the mall was being marketed, although their firm had yet to approach the Villar group about a deal.

In a disclosure on Friday, October 30, Vista Malls said it had “not accepted any binding offer or entered into any definitive agreement” to sell Santa Rosa. It also said it does not comment on “preliminary, exploratory, or non-binding discussions.”

VistaREIT, another listed company in the group, offered its own narrow clarification, saying there was no definitive transaction involving a transfer of the assets into the real estate investment trust. Vista Land, meanwhile, said it was continually assessing property disposals and options to manage its liquidity.

In its 2025 audited financial statements, released only this October, Vista Land said it had already entered into agreements to dispose of unspecified investment properties after year-end and that the transactions were not recognized in the current set of financials. No properties were specifically identified. (READ: Villar’s Vista Land 2025 net income falls 59% as delayed figures surface)
Carefully chosen words, but none rule out talking to potential buyers.
Could these moves be coming as the Villars struggle to raise cash to meet billions in debt obligations due very soon?
