articles.title: 'You can't just get out': How 2 boys were recruited into the drug trade at the age of 12
articles.byline: Aliyah Marko-Omene, Shelley Ayres, Mark Kelley, Danielle Reid

image.caption: Teen boys across Canada are being lured to work on the front lines of a lucrative and dangerous drug trade in remote communities, CBC's the fifth estate has found. (Shelley Ayres/CBC)

blocks.text: Kai was 12 years old when he began to warn his mother he might not make it home.
"[If] I don't make it home by four o'clock, just know that I got snatched and somebody put me in their car and kidnapped me," he would tell her.

His mother, whom CBC's the fifth estate is calling Aria for her protection, moved her family to another city when Kai was a boy to disconnect from his father, who had a criminal past and street associations.
She enrolled Kai, whose name has also been changed for his protection, in community centres and drop-in spaces in Winnipeg to keep him busy and away from trouble
But Aria believes those spaces exposed her son to people who would exploit him.

items: Watch the full documentary, "Missing Boys: Lured into Danger," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

blocks.text: She believes some staff abused their positions, allowing gang members to manipulate her son and coerce him into the drug trade — sending him thousands of kilometres away from home.

Fifth estate host Mark Kelley, left, sits down with a boy who was recruited by a gang when he was 12. He says he has been sent out of town to sell drugs more times than he can count. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Kai said men in their 20s and 30s presented themselves as people he could trust.
"People call it grooming, people call it using. There's many words for it, but it's just being taken advantage of because you're innocent," Kai said.

For the last two years, the fifth estate has investigated the disappearances of young Black boys from the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) who are groomed and lured into drug trafficking networks in Ontario cities as far away as Sarnia and Thunder Bay, and sent further north into Indigenous communities like Ginoogaming, a First Nation.

items: How gangs lure Black boys to northern Ontario 'trap houses'

blocks.text: Now, the fifth estate has heard directly from boys who live this dangerous life and say they were sent across the country to sell drugs, revealing a network that reaches even farther.

We now know of this activity taking boys as young as 12 as far west as British Columbia, as far north as Yellowknife and as far east as Halifax — places where drugs are sold at exponentially higher prices — up to 10 times the price in some cases.
The business of going OT
In an interview with CBC's the fifth estate, Kai recounts his first trip out of town, also known as “going OT,” when he was 12.
"You don't know what's in those bags. You don't know what you're delivering for people … you just think, 'I'm helping the older guy, because I want to be cool like him,'" he said.
Kai said the older men picked him up, told him where he would stay and expected him to sell drugs. He was left in a remote community eight hours north of his home in Winnipeg.
LISTEN: The Missing Boys: When It All Went Wrong
Kai said he did not fully understand what he was getting into. He had to figure it out in a place where he did not know anyone and his family was out of reach.
"You're not telling family members," he said. "Because not only do they not know where you are, you don't know where you are."
The first trip taught him more about what he calls the rules of "the game," where the three outcomes are freedom, jail or death.
And he says he was forced to gamble for the gangs.
"You can't just get out ... whoever sent you there is expecting you to come back with a prize," Kai said. "And if you don't come back with anything … God forbid something happens to you."
Now 14, Kai has made more trips out of town than he can count.
On the front line of the drug trade
Jamal, another teenager whose name has been changed for his safety, started going OT at 12. He had been away from home for more than a week and his mom reported him missing.
The now-18-year-old who lives in the Toronto area said he has been sent to communities in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario.
Jamal's farthest trip took him to Yellowknife. He was even convinced to pay his own way.

Like Kai, Jamal said it was in Grade 7 when he was first approached to work for a gang. His family had spent a year bouncing between houses and he grew close to older people in his neighbourhood who were often around his cousins.
"I always just had the respect and looked at them like an older role model," he said.
Jamal said those role models could offer him an escape from the instability at home.

items: Searching for Ontario’s missing Black boys
Calls to stem violence in northern First Nations as Ginoogaming man’s family mourns shooting death

blocks.text: "If things were stable at home, I wouldn't really have a reason to go outside," he said.
Jamal said the adults he worked for were selling drugs bought internationally — and worked with cartels.

Then Jamal tells the fifth estate how the boys cross the country — a key piece of information — as many families are baffled as to how their boys are boarding planes and driving to remote locations when they are too young to have a driver's licence and don't have identification.
Jamal said fake names and identification are provided for them.
"It doesn't even matter who you are, how young you are. You can go anywhere in Canada," he said. "It's actually quite easy."
The adults behind the operation
The fifth estate previously found adult traffickers use the boys as disposable mules and legal shields that often take the fall when police make drug busts.

A 2026 federal Justice Department report found that the proportion of Black youth in correctional supervision in Nova Scotia, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia remained at around 12 to 13 per cent from 2019 to 2024. That's almost two times more than their combined share of the population for that age group, across all four provinces.

Black boys often face well-known socio-economic challenges including high unemployment, and bias within justice and educational systems that can make them more vulnerable to the pull of organized crime.
"Many of these youth[s] are exploited … they're seen as disposable to the people who are running these networks," said Winnipeg police Insp. Josh Ewatski.

Winnipeg police Insp. Josh Ewatski tells the fifth estate the drugs supplied by gangs have been linked to international cartels. Young boys are often used for street-level dealing so gang members don't have to expose themselves to violence or being arrested. (Oliver Walters/CBC)
In May, Ewatski led a team involved in what police called Manitoba's largest drug bust. Investigators seized 525 kilograms of cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl in Winnipeg.
Those arrested included people associated with Canada's highest ranks of organized crime including the Hells Angels, Wolfpack Alliance and a Mexican cartel.
"Most of the drugs of cocaine and methamphetamine will come from Mexico up to the U.S. and into Canada," Ewatski said.
He described a sophisticated network where multiple drug trafficking organizations are working together to move drugs into remote communities.
He says it's associates of these international criminal networks who are recruiting and using boys.
Ewatski said boys are used for street-level dealing and to work in stash houses. He said they often don't know who they are working for.
"These kids are used so [those running the networks] don't have to expose themselves to being arrested or being shot."
Leaving a gang can be just as dangerous. Ewatski said some boys become trapped by debts they are told they owe their recruiters.
“If they're out, they're going to be out in a violent way," he said. "Possibly even dead."
Denny Heathen, a reformed gang member, now counsels youth and leads prayer circles in his community of Prince Albert, Sask. (Shelley Ayres/CBC)

Denny Heathen spent much of his 20s working for a gang in Prince Albert, Sask. He said some recruiters targeted boys between 15 to 18 and told us that the boys who were targeted had a look of desperation.
"They wanted purpose," Heathen said.
Recruiters offered attention, money and the promise of protection, presenting themselves as brothers or older mentors.
"These are puppets," he said. "You just got to make them feel like they're appreciated, like they are going to be taken care of."
What it takes to get out of a gang
Kai remembers the grooming process well.
“You're a little kid in a community centre trying to play basketball and then you see these guys … walking around with the large prize in their hand."
The prize was money — an amount that felt impossible to a boy too young to get his first job.
During his interview with the fifth estate, Kai pulled out a thick stack of $100 bills to demonstrate how quickly money could influence a boy to sell drugs.
"All it takes is this and you're influenced."
He said the amounts involved can be enormous in First Nations communities where an oxycodone pill can sell for $200.
"That substance that is being put in these boys' pockets and these boys' hands to go deal over the province … people will do anything for."
The boy who never came home
On March 27, 2025, Jay'siiah Webb-Long walked out of his family's home in Brampton, Ont., carrying a single duffel bag that appeared nearly empty.

Doorbell camera footage provided by the family to the fifth estate shows the 15-year-old placing a single box in the recycling bin on his front porch, scanning the street before disappearing out of frame.
His story made national headlines.
Jay'siiah Webb-Long, 15, was last seen outside his home in Brampton, Ont. on March 27, 2025. (Saskatchewan RCMP)
"Somebody had sent me photos after his disappearance," said Shenice Long, his mother.
"She had sent photos of him holding stacks of money. So, at that point, I said, 'OK, somebody has sent him far out … to make money.'"
Long said she remained in contact with her son for weeks after he left home. But he would not tell her where he was.

Jay'siiah's family told the fifth estate they are frustrated with action from Peel Regional Police and the RCMP in Saskatchewan, citing for example that it took Peel police eight weeks to alert the public that Jay'siiah was missing.

Long said police used a phone number she never had for her son to trace his location to Pelican Narrows, Sask., a northern community about 3,000 kilometres from his home in Brampton. This number only surfaced when the public alert came out and a young woman came forward.
"I heard of Saskatchewan, but … I don't have family there. I don't know anyone there," Long said.
In July 2025, Saskatchewan RCMP took over the file as a homicide investigation. They didn't alert the public of this shift until September 2025.
Police told the family a search was delayed by winter weather. In the spring, investigators told the family they planned to search near Pelican Narrows — led with cadaver dogs.
Pelican Narrows, Sask., a community of about 4,000 and located about 500 kilometres north of Saskatoon, is part of the Peter Ballantyne Cree Nation. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
On May 13, human remains were found near a sewage lagoon just outside the community. An autopsy confirmed two days later that the remains belonged to Webb-Long.
RCMP believe his death was a homicide. The investigation is ongoing and no charges have been laid in connection with his death.
Missing — and not always reported

In 2024, 322 male youth were reported missing to Toronto police. Statistics Canada data shows Black boys account for almost half of those missing, despite representing less than 10 per cent of the city's population of that age group.

The fifth estate has found not every family reports their youth missing. In the case of Jay'siiah Webb-Long, his mother didn't file a formal report until three weeks after he had left home. She told the fifth estate she had called Peel Regional Police after 48 hours but they dissuaded her because she was still in contact with him.

"One youth missing is too [many]," said Christene Lewis, who is a violence intervention specialist and works with families in Toronto and surrounding areas. She supports many families who have youth that go missing and go "OT." It's a life she knows because she lived it.
"I come from the gang culture," Lewis said. "I come from feeling isolated, I've come from feeling like the streets were more loyal to me than my own family was."
Christene Lewis, a violence intervention specialist, works with families in Toronto and surrounding areas who have youth who go missing. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Lewis said some parents hesitate reporting their child missing because they fear their kids will be treated as runaways rather than young people at risk. Others feel shame and embarrassment.
Lewis said there is also a breakdown of trust between marginalized communities and police.
"They don't feel like the police even care."
Lewis's advice to parents: Always report a missing kid and keep following up.
"If they didn't hear you the first day, call the next day," she said. "Don't give up."
A message for parents of missing kids
Aria remembers when it first became clear her son had gone to a First Nations community to sell drugs.
"He was telling stories like he came back from camp," she said.
He would leave home sporadically, returning home with designer clothing and money.
Aria said she has also had the windows of her home shot at three times.
Now, when Kai goes missing, she reports him and collects evidence that might help police locate him.
"This is not something you make peace with," she said. "This is something that's wrong."
'Nobody's just going to let you go'
Jamal said the people who recruited him continue to contact him and tell him he owes them money.
''They're going to keep texting you, telling you that they got this opportunity … nobody's just going to let you just go."
Kai has also tried to leave. He spent the summer away at camp and returned determined to get out of gang life.
"Now that I realize what kind of hell on earth is like … I never want to go back there," he told the fifth estate in August.
But Aria said the messages continued.
She found text messages about Kai from a sibling that read: "I will not be returning your little bro" and "he's my slave.”
She believes the messages are proof her son is being trafficked.
Aria, a Winnipeg mother whose name has been changed for protection, worries gangs will never loosen their grip on her son. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Kai left home again the night before he was set to start Grade 10. He returned home and left again several times.
Aria fears that even if Kai manages to break free from the gangs, they will continue to chase and manipulate him, tempting him with money and a sense of belonging.
Kai is facing drug trafficking charges.
"This monster exists and it's going to exist on his path as a young man, as an adult," Aria said. "I don't think that this monster ever goes away."

articles.title: Why the war in Iran might cost Trump and the Republicans at the ballot box
articles.summary: When Americans head to the ballot box, it is usually domestic issues that are at the front of mind, not foreign policy. But this time, Americans are linking the high price of gas and diesel with the…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump attends a midterm campaign rally to support Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·Analysis

When Americans head to the ballot box, it is usually domestic issues that are at the front of mind, not foreign policy. But this time, Americans are linking the high price of gas and diesel with the U.S. war in the Middle East.
The conflict has driven oil prices up and that's hitting Americans at the pumps

When U.S. and Israeli jets flew east on Feb. 28, striking hundreds of targets across Iran and killing much of the country's leadership, they also inadvertently catapulted the world into an oil crisis that persists today and that just might cost U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican colleagues during next week's midterm elections.
Historically, the midterms are seen as a referendum on the president and his party.
More often than not, the party that controls the White House loses ground in the House and Senate.

The polls currently predict Democrats taking control of the House, while the Senate remains too close to call. Republicans hold a four-seat majority giving them room to lose, while still retaining control of the upper chamber. This cycle, 33 seats are up for grabs, Republicans currently hold 20 of them, while Democrats hold the remaining 13.
When Americans head to the ballot box, it is usually domestic issues that are at the front of mind, not foreign policy.

Foreign policy "is very distant for people," said Clifford Young, chair of Ipsos Public Affairs. "Ultimately what they care about are their pocketbooks and how they get along in their day-to-day lives and the two things are often fairly separate in people's minds and voters' minds."
But Young says, this time, Americans are linking the high price of gas and diesel with U.S. actions in the Middle East.
Gas prices are shown at a gas station in Atlanta, Ga., on Friday. (Edgar Su/Reuters)

On Feb. 27, the day before the U.S. and Israel kickstarted their war against Iran, the price of oil was $67 US per barrel. By March 1 the price had jumped to $99 US per barrel and it has stayed pretty close to that for the eight months since.
That has caused the average price of gas in the U.S. to climb from $2.98 US per gallon to $4.25 US per gallon, according to data compiled by the American Automobile Association.

"These have been decisions that [Trump's] made on the foreign policy side that have significantly impacted Americans domestically and more specifically his political bailiwick, his own base," said Young.
"Trump made a decision that significantly eroded his political capital domestically."
Indeed, according to a Reuters Ipsos poll published earlier this month, 78 per cent of people surveyed blame Trump's policies for rising prices in general.
Supporters attend the rally for Paxton in Lubbock, on Tuesday. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)
The Republican and MAGA base previously rallied around Trump's "America First" agenda, which in part involved a promise to extricate the country from foreign conflicts.
At first, the administration said the war with Iran would only last four to six weeks. But despite an overwhelming military display, the U.S. has been unable to end it.

"It was a war of discretion, a war of choice, launched without any thought to the capacity of the administration's hand in order to reach its objectives," said Aaron David Miller, a former U.S. Middle East negotiator, who is now a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

"It completely underestimated the capacity of the adversary to respond and escalate horizontally and weaponize geography, and to basically go after the vulnerabilities of the Straight of Hormuz and the Gulf states."
The war has become increasingly unpopular with Americans — according to the Pew Research Center, nearly two-third of Americans disapprove of it.

Fire and smoke rise from the Fujairah oil industry zone, caused by debris after interception of a drone by air defences, according to the Fujairah media office, amid the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran, in Fujairah, U.A.E., on March 4. (Amr Alfiky/Reuters)
That survey reveals that while the conflict has been broadly unpopular from the start it has grown even less popular with Republicans and Republican-leaning independents.

Of course, Trump's foreign policy extends beyond the U.S. war with Iran, and he has seen other wins and losses. He recently helped to secure the release of the remaining hostages held by Hamas in Gaza and brokered a fragile ceasefire between that militant group and Israel.
A resident stands at the site of an apartment building damaged during a Russian jet drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kharkiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 12. (Sofiia Gatilova/Reuters)

And, in a daring military operation, U.S. forces captured Venezuela's longtime President Nicolás Maduro and flew him to the U.S. where he currently faces a slew of federal charges. Washington has subsequently been working closely with Maduro's Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez, who is now the interim president.

He has also had a fractious relationship with NATO allies including Canada, and has pivoted the U.S. away from Ukraine — recently lifting sanctions on Russia, in an effort to bring down the price of oil and diesel.

And yet, a recent poll by Marist/NPR/PBS News found that foreign policy overall was the top issue for only five per cent of Americans surveyed. Thirty-four percent said cost of living was the number one issue driving their vote.

items: These midterm races will decide who controls U.S. Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency
Election denial has gone mainstream in the U.S. What does that mean for the midterms?

blocks.text: And that’s where we see the convergence — unusual for a U.S. election — of foreign policy and domestic affordability issues.

It is the war in Iran that is likely to cost Trump most. The question of affordability is front and centre this midterm cycle and the price of gas is a glaring reminder of Trump's decision to start a conflict that previous presidents had avoided.

Two Blocks from the White House36:47Your questions about the U.S. midterms, answered
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Willy Lowry is an award-winning correspondent for CBC News in Washington, D.C., where he provides breaking news and analysis across radio and television. Prior to that, he served as the senior U.S. correspondent at the National newspaper in D.C., where he covered the U.S. State Department, American foreign policy and its impacts on the Middle East and the wider world. Willy covered the Israel-Hamas war extensively, travelling to Israel and the occupied West Bank several times. He also covered the fall of ISIS in Syria. He started his career at CBC News in Montreal, where he worked his way up from intern to research assistant and eventually to video journalist.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Accused sex predator Richard Neil disputes DNA link to Ontario crime scenes
articles.summary: A Toronto man accused of grisly attacks on children in public parks in southern Ontario in the 1990s repeatedly this week disputed evidence against him and insisted police arrested the wrong man.

image.caption: Richard Neil leaves a Brampton, Ont., courthouse on Oct. 16. The 67-year-old is on trial for a series of sex assaults against children in the 1990s. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·New
A Toronto man accused of grisly attacks on children in public parks in southern Ontario in the 1990s repeatedly this week disputed evidence against him and insisted police arrested the wrong man.
'It's not me,' Neil tells court as trial for string of 1990s assaults continues
WARNING: This story contains details of sexual assaults against children
"It's not my DNA," Richard Neil testified at his trial in Brampton. "It's not me."
Crown prosecutors say DNA evidence links Neil to crime scenes in Kitchener, Brampton and Oakville, three decades after the "woodland attacker" case baffled investigators.

Two boys, aged eight and 10, and a 15-year-old girl each told police they'd been lured into wooded areas, tied up and raped by a stranger. The victims all said they'd been forced to drink the assailant's urine during the attacks, which occurred between 1992 and 1995.

The jury heard Neil wasn't arrested until March 2024, after forensic genetic genealogy pointed to him as a suspect. Prosecutors said further laboratory analysis found it's "20 quadrillion times more likely" that the DNA at the crime scenes belonged to Neil, rather than another, random person.
DNA on underwear worn as mask helped identify alleged child rapist
"I'm not a scientist," he said from the Ontario Superior Court of Justice witness box on Tuesday, according to an audio recording reviewed by CBC News.
"All I can say is it was not me. I had nothing to do with it."
Neil, 67, has pleaded not guilty to the 17 charges including kidnapping, sexual assault causing bodily harm and administering a stupefying drug.
Assistant Crown attorney Monica MacKenzie said it was an "impossible coincidence" that multiple pieces of evidence — including fingerprints — also connect Neil to the three attacks.
The jury was previously told Neil's fingerprints were lifted from two shopping bags and a two-litre pop bottle located at Wildwood Park in Oakville, where the girl was assaulted in August 1995.
An 'interest in urine'
During her cross-examination, MacKenzie also zeroed in on the accused's "interest in urine."
Neil acknowledged that he developed a urine-drinking "fetish" around 2012, insisting "it's actually quite common."
"Anytime I've engaged in that act," he said, "it's been with consenting male adults only."

The court heard the British-born Neil immigrated to Canada with his family as a child. He grew up in Kitchener, where the first boy was assaulted in the city's Idlewood Park, in August 1992. At the time, the jury was told Neil had a home in neighbouring Waterloo.
He spent much of his career working as a Toronto-area driver for employers such as Canada Post, UPS and Bell.

MacKenzie, the prosecutor, said Neil happened to be unemployed when the first two attacks — in Kitchener in 1992 and in Brampton's Norton Place Park in September 1994 — occurred. She said at the time of the 1995 Oakville attack, Neil's job involved delivering phone books and that he had a "very loose schedule."

The jury was shown this image of a two-litre pop bottle recovered from the scene of a brutal attack in Oakville, Ont., in 1995. The 15-year-old victim told police the unknown assailant forced her to drink urine from the bottle. (Ontario Superior Court of Justice)
When he was arrested in 2024, Neil was splitting his time between his Toronto condo and a house in Victoria. The court previously heard officers searched both addresses after he was detained.
Neil testified that he was awoken from a nap when police showed up at his door in Toronto to arrest him and seize his electronic devices.
Previously detained, not fingerprinted
Once DNA evidence had linked all three assaults in the 1990s, forensic scientists looked at roughly 310 persons of interest over the years, a witness previously testified.
It appears likely they would not have had Neil's DNA or fingerprints in their database, or his name on their list of suspects, at the time.
Other than traffic violations, the court heard Neil had only one previous run-in with police.

He testified that he was 19 years old when he and another man had been detained for "two, three hours, tops" for a drinking offence in Toronto. They weren't charged and officers didn't take their fingerprints, Neil said.

items: Boy recounts 1994 park attack on tape played at trial
Jury hears forensic expert in cold case sex assault trial
Crown says DNA evidence helped ID man now on trial for decades-old sex assaults against children

blocks.text: The jury also previously heard contemporaneous police interviews of the three victims, who were not required to testify at trial. The Crown and defence both agreed the attacks took place as the children described at the time.
"There's no quarrel as to what occurred, or that these crimes took place," Neil's defence lawyer, Leo Adler told the jury.
"The issue has been from the start, who is the individual responsible."
Neil, a divorced father of three, is set to resume his testimony on Friday.

In September 1994, a 10-year-old boy told police he was walking through Brampton's Norton Place Park, when he was approached by a stranger and lured to a nearby wooded area where he was sexually assaulted. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Thomas is a CBC News reporter based in Toronto. In recent years, he has covered some of the biggest stories in the world, from the 2015 Paris attacks to the Tokyo Olympics and the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II. He's reported from the Lac-Mégantic rail disaster, the Freedom Convoy protest in Ottawa and the Pope's visit to Canada aimed at reconciliation with Indigenous people. Thomas can be reached at thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.
With files from Dana Roberts

articles.title: Apple TV's Nocturne is Nordic noir by the numbers
articles.summary: Apple TV's Nocturne has just enough serviceable storytelling and professionally lit scenes to lull you into habit-viewing. But after several episodes of uninspired reveals you might suddenly come to…

image.caption: Stephen Graham appears in a still from Apple TV's Nocturne. (Apple TV)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

Apple TV's Nocturne has just enough serviceable storytelling and professionally lit scenes to lull you into habit-viewing. But after several episodes of uninspired reveals you might suddenly come to your senses and ask: "Wait, why am I watching this?"
Stephen Graham's foreboding villain can't elevate this series above genre's complex and macabre conventions
If it wasn't for Adolescence star Stephen Graham's involvement as a mendacious, menacing serial killer, you likely wouldn't have heard of Nocturne.

Then again — this being an Apple TV show after all — you might not have heard of it anyway. Not to say the streaming also-ran doesn't have at least some must-watch TV: just ask your friends obsessed with Slow Horses or obsessively awaiting just one more season of Severance.
But for every Ted Lasso, there seem to be two or three Cape Fears: standard streaming-fare releases that, while high budget and adequately designed, don't do much to demand viewing.

If you do choose to amble through, there is just enough serviceable storytelling and professionally lit scenes to lull you into habit-viewing. It's only after several episodes of uninspired reveals you suddenly come to your senses and ask: "Wait, why am I watching this?"

Which could function as the be-all-end-all description of Nocturne. Adapted from crime novels The Sandman and Lazarus by Lars Kepler, it follows the conventions of its "Nordic noir" progenitors to a painful T.

First, we have a typically unsettling mystery. Who could be kidnapping people and burying them alive with just enough food and water to ensure they die slowly? And why have they seemingly released young Michael (Landon Valentin), who is discovered stumbling back into town years after he and his sister disappeared?

The No. 1 suspect would be Jurek Walter (Graham), given he was convicted for exactly these types of crimes long ago. However, aside from using his borderline supernatural powers of manipulation to convince his cellmate to bash his head into the wall, Walter hasn't had much of an opportunity to make a nuisance of himself lately. And, of course, there's the fact he's been locked up in a psychiatric hospital for years.

So then there is the attempt to uncover the mystery, all mixed up with the necessary pathos and a dizzyingly interconnected cast of characters. There is Jonah Lynn (Liev Schreiber), the damaged ex-cop responsible for putting Walter away in the first place. There's FBI agent and undercover specialist Saga Bauer (Zazie Beetz) — Lynn's surrogate daughter tasked with posing as a patient to get closer to Walter.

items: Stop-motion movie Wildwood is a staggering masterpiece. It's a miracle it exists at all

blocks.text: Then there's the nervous but well-meaning nurse Karl (Rory Culkin), secretly delivering Walter's letters to his lawyer while obviously falling under the killer's carefully orchestrated spell. And there's also functional FBI agent/dysfunctional mom Alexandra Quinn (Poorna Jagannathan); bumbling but committed police chief Dave Ellison (Bill Camp); and Michael's fiercely committed but floundering mom Ida (Chrissy Metz).

All are plagued by past trauma and lingering, all-consuming pain. And all are involved in the complicated, interweaving plot to find Michael's sister Felicia before she runs out of time in her box below the dirt — assuming she's not already dead.
Zazie Beetz as Saga Bauer in a still from Nocturne. (Apple TV)

And so the "complicated" and "macabre" prerequisites for Nordic noir are satisfied. Transplanted from the books' Swedish setting to a small town in Pennsylvania, the brooding and bleak esthetics still jump to the fore. No one is allowed on screen without a broken and haunted expression.

Not a day is allowed to go by without oppressive, grey colour-grading — making the sky appear to constantly be seconds away from releasing a torrential downpour. And not a single attempt at well-meaning altruism is allowed to go unpunished by a vindictive, cruel universe — at least in the first two episodes of the 10-part series released Friday.

items: Queen of Canada documentary director wants you to know her followers are still out there

blocks.text: For all its considerable cliché, Nocturne is elevated by Graham. There is something uniquely menacing about what is clearly a Hannibal Lecter descendant: a chameleonic svengali who at times appears so emotionally blunted you wonder if he's actually awake; and who, at other times, gives such an entrancing performance of empathy you genuinely begin to wonder how easily such a monster could come to control you.

On the one hand, Graham's committedly unsettling performance offers at least one somewhat original aspect to Nocturne; on the other, the torturously subdued evocation of evil doesn't do much for the show's drama. It may put Walter in the running against No Country for Old Men's Anton Chigurh as the most realistic psychopath put to screen; but it does not put him in the running as the most entertaining.

As the show ping-pongs between interconnected storylines — and refuses to go as campily overwrought as the Hannibal series, from which Nocturne obviously borrows — Walter's weird, clown-like guffaws and subtle hints at violent intentions tend to get lost in the weeds.

items: Netflix's Adolescence is making parents panic about what kids do online — but should they be?

blocks.text: What comes through more is the aimless voyeurism of the other genre Nocturne apes: true crime.

Graham himself detailed his research process as binging crime documentaries, while Apple TV opted to advertise the show in a similar way. "If you like true crime, you'll love this show," ad after ad claims; a testimonial Nocturne seems designed to satisfy.

That's because — completely separate from any debate about the ethics of mining crime for entertainment — the vast majority of true crime releases suffer from the same problem: gussying up incidental crimes as universally consequential and then artificially stretching out the mystery behind them to pad out an overlong end product.

As more and more characters stumble into an improbably interwoven crime, Nocturne feels ever more like a documentary you just never bothered to finish. Assuming the series follows the general plot of the novels, it all leads to a laughably predictable reveal — one that would make skipping the most time-conscious choice.

With only two episodes available, it may be too early to say. Nocturne's slow-burn start may evolve into something worthwhile, while Graham's performance and the tantalizing mystery at Nocturne's heart do offer just enough intrigue to draw you in.
Although, if you really wanted a good time, The Silence of the Lambs is right there.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Indigenous women could make history in upcoming U.S. midterm elections
articles.summary: Deb Haaland is running for governor of New Mexico, while Mary Peltola, Peggy Flanagan and N'kiyla (Jasmine) Thomas are running for seats in the U.S. Senate. No Indigenous woman has ever been elected…

image.caption: Deb Haaland speaks June 2 during a primary election night watch party after winning the Democratic nomination to run for governor, in Albuquerque, N.M. (Jon Austria/Associated Press)

blocks.text: Indigenous

Deb Haaland is running for governor of New Mexico, while Mary Peltola, Peggy Flanagan and N'kiyla (Jasmine) Thomas are running for seats in the U.S. Senate. No Indigenous woman has ever been elected to either role.
In some states with close races, Indigenous voters could be deciding factor, say experts
Indigenous women could make history in the U.S. midterm elections next week.

Deb Haaland is running for governor of New Mexico, while Mary Peltola, Peggy Flanagan and N'kiyla (Jasmine) Thomas are running for seats in the U.S. Senate. No Indigenous woman has ever been elected to either role, but that could change on Nov. 3.

Haaland, a Democrat and member of the Laguna Pueblo, was one of two Native American women elected to Congress in 2018. Two years later she became the first Indigenous person to serve as secretary of the Interior — the department that manages the nation's natural resources, cultural heritage sites, and works with Native Americans on treaty obligations — a post she held until 2025.
Now Haaland has set her sights on the New Mexico governorship.

Data collected by Advanced Native Political Leadership (ANPL) and shared with CBC News, shows at least 359 Native American, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian candidates are running for public office across 36 states in 2026, compared to 268 across 25 states in 2024.
The majority are running for local office. Of the Indigenous candidates running on the federal ticket, half are women.

Jordan James Harvill, a member of the Cherokee Nation and descendant of the Choctaw Nation, is senior director of national programs for ANPL — an Indigenous-led organization that works to increase Indigenous representation in public office, through training, research and programming.
He said women comprise up to 80 per cent of applications for ANPL leadership programs.

"It just happens to be that Native women are the ones who are doing a lot of the work in community and so they are the ones who were best positioned to run for office and represent the community when the time comes," Harvill said.
Mary Peltola, a Democrat running for the U.S. Senate seat in Alaska, addresses supporters on Aug. 18 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Mark Thiessen/Associated Press)
It appears the leadership programs are paying off. Harvill said Native American women who run for office are outperforming men.
"They're running and winning at something around 10 percentage points higher than men overall," Harvill said.
Many of the women hoping to make history with a seat in the U.S. Senate have already broken glass ceilings.

Peltola, who is Yup'ik, is the Democratic candidate running to represent Alaska in the U.S. Senate. She's already made history as the first Alaska Native person elected to Congress and the first woman to hold Alaska’s House seat.

Flanagan, a Democrat hoping to represent Minnesota in the U.S. Senate, is the lieutenant governor of Minnesota, making her the current highest-ranking Indigenous woman elected to executive office in the U.S. She is Ojibway and a member of White Earth Nation.
Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic lieutenant governor of Minnesota, has her sights set on the U.S. Senate. (Ellen Schmidt/Associated Press)
Thomas, a Democrat, is a Chickasaw citizen with no political history who is running for U.S. Senate in Oklahoma.
Harvill said that according to ANPL's research, nearly half of all Native American candidates over the last five years have won their races.
"Which is a pretty high win rate overall, particular for many of them who are running in some of the most competitive and challenging districts in the United States," Harvill said.
Native American voters could be 'deciding factor'
There are 4.7 million eligible Native American voters in the U.S., according to a report from the Native American Rights Fund (NARF).
According to the report, only 66 per cent of eligible Indigenous voters are registered.
"I believe that Native people are the most significant voting block in the country and will determine the president in 2028," Harvill said.
Allison Neswood, a member of the Navajo Nation and senior staff attorney at NARF, said who is in power both at the federal and local level "can be very much influenced by Native voters."
Navajo attorney Allison Neswood, is senior staff attorney at the Native American Rights Fund. (Cliff Owen/Associated Press)
Neswood said Native American voters in states such as Arizona and Wisconsin can determine the outcome of elections.
"It's not the whole ball game for sure, but it's certainly one of the leverage pieces that our communities have and in the fight for our rights," Neswood said.

OJ Semans, a member of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe in South Dakota and executive director of Four Directions Native Vote - Indian Country, said Native Americans have significant leverage in states such as Wisconsin, Michigan, Nevada and Georgia and "have the power to decide who is going to sit in D.C."
Candidates in these states won by slim margins in recent federal elections, he said, and the number of Indigenous people of voting age in those states exceeds the winning margins.
"If we're able to mobilize and get Natives to the polls, they could actually be the deciding factor in who gets elected," Semans said.
All political stripes
Jean Schroedel, a professor emerita of political science at Claremont Graduate University in Clairmont, Calif., said when it comes to voting preference, Indigenous people run the gamut.

"When you talk about Indigenous people in the United States, they go from extremely conservative MAGA [Make America Great Again], all the way to DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] and every place in between," Schroedel said.
Francine Bradley-Arthur, a Navajo, stands in front of Freedom House, a grassroots pro-Trump campaign house she founded on the Navajo Nation in Window Rock, Ariz., in 2024. (AP)

Francine Bradley-Arthur, for example, is Navajo and a former Democrat. She said she began to campaign for President Donald Trump in part because she felt Native American communities in Arizona often didn’t feel the payoff despite longtime support for her former party.
The current secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, former senator Markwayne Mullin, is a member of the Cherokee Nation and a MAGA stalwart.

items: Indigenous leaders urge citizens to carry status cards or tribal IDs in U.S.
2 Native American-owned corporations cancel contracts with ICE

blocks.text: "All those deportations and things that are going on as we speak are under his watch," Schoroedel said.
"He's in charge."

Two Native American incumbent Republicans will also be running for the House of Representatives in Oklahoma: Tom Cole, a member of the Chickasaw Nation, and Josh Brecheen, a member of the Choctaw Nation.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jackie McKay is a Métis journalist working for CBC Indigenous covering B.C., and winner of a 2025 Canadian Screen Award for best local reporter. She was a reporter for CBC North for more than five years spending the majority of her time in Nunavut. McKay has also worked in Whitehorse, Thunder Bay, and Yellowknife.

Cost of Living5:09Why your Halloween candy disappears before the first doorbell ring

Jessica Ryan needs to buy a lot of candy each year. She runs a children's consignment store in Windsor, Ont., and the surrounding neighbourhood hosts a Halloween party, where she sees up to a thousand kids, all looking for sweet, sweet candy.
This year, she bought her Halloween candy early. But before she knew it, a box had already not-so-mysteriously vanished.
"I have four children, so that box was gone in like five minutes."

It wasn't long before Ryan was down four boxes of candy. And she's not the only one seeing her candy disappear earlier. According to an Ipsos survey commissioned by Hello Products in 2023, the most recent figures available, more than half of the 1,282 Canadian adults surveyed at the time said they had to restock before Oct. 31.
Analysts credit this to clever packaging and marketing, along with the big boxes of candy showing up earlier and earlier each year.
Jessica Ryan bought 16 boxes of candy when it went on sale. But a few of the boxes have already been depleted. (Submitted by Jessica Ryan)
In other words, if you buy a box of candy in August, it's going to be tough to resist the temptation until October.

“The season has definitely become longer and shopping behaviour has expanded right along with it,” said Sally Lyons Wyatt, who follows food trends for the global research firm Circana and is based in Texas.
Halloween creep
Lyons Wyatt says it used to be that Halloween candy sales primarily took place in September and October.
But Halloween candy is now hitting shelves well before the leaves start to fall, with some stores stocking the sweet treats while it's still prime beach weather, a nod to the “Summerween” trend.
While having those sweet treats in stores early doesn't guarantee you will buy candy early, it does give you an opportunity, says Conor Lane.
"What putting it earlier allows [stores] to do is maximize their number of dice rolls," said Lane, a neuroscientist with The Decision Lab, a consumer behaviour research firm in Montreal.
Halloween candy has been showing up on store shelves earlier and earlier, says Sally Lyons Wyatt. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

"They have a much higher chance of getting you on a day where you've had a really tough day and you just want something to make your day a bit better, or you're in an extremely good mood and you think you might just want to treat yourself."
Lyons Wyatt says the latter is indicative of consumers increasingly looking for experiences and moments of joy.

A 2026 survey, conducted by Ipsos for the Mars company, which produces Mars bars, M&Ms and Skittles, found that nearly half of the 1,000 Canadians surveyed believed Halloween was no longer a single day, but rather a full season.
A similar survey by Mars in the U.S. also found that many Gen Z respondents were baking spooky treats and attending Halloween parties while still in the summer months.
"Summerween checks all those boxes. It's fun. It's creative. It's social, family-friendly, and relatively affordable compared to a lot of other forms of entertainment," said Lyons Wyatt.
Cues and learned associations
But early stocking isn't the only reason why some customers are buying sooner, Lane says. There are also some simple marketing tricks.
He says candy sells because of cues and learned associations.
“There is essentially an entire industry built around stimulating your cravings.”
There's the bright-coloured packaging that makes it impossible to miss. That's the cue. The learned association is that when we see candy, we think yummy.
“It works so well that we're even willing to eat a lot of Halloween candy, despite the fact that we know it's usually not very good quality," said Lane.
And then there's the bite-size nature of Halloween treats.
"Each little piece feels like it barely counts," said Lane. “It allows us to go over our kind of natural point of, 'Oh, I should stop here. I've eaten a whole chocolate bar.'"
Some Canadians no longer view Halloween as just a single day for candy, but rather an entire season of its own. (Michael Conroy/Associated Press)
In need of a restock
So what do you do if you find yourself low on Halloween candy as the children start to arrive in their Elsa and Buzz Lightyear costumes?
Ryan has found herself in that exact pickle, and has had to get creative.
"The kids go out with their friends or whoever comes home first, I'm like, 'Give me what you guys aren't going to eat and I'll hand them back out to the other kids.'"
Or, you can do what candy-makers are banking on.
“I’m probably going to grab more," said Ryan. “I'm sure we're going to eat another box or two before Halloween.”

articles.title: The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism
articles.summary: From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

image.caption: The hot dog costume for the sausage dog is a classic at the annual Paris Sausage WalkImage: Folglio Antoine/ABACA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.
Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited the painter at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.
The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

blocks.caption: The exhibition includes installations created for dogsImage: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with his adoptive pet.
A particularly iconic animal

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.
Germany's 'badger dog'

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

blocks.caption: A lithography from 1867 showing children feeding deer with a dachshund watchingImage: Wolfgang Diederich/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.
Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.
An evolving cultural icon
Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.
Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, while the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the First World War because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

blocks.caption: Described as the 'Devil dog' in US propaganda from 1917Image: akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet Of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Dobermann, or dogs that looked big and dangerous."
A symbol of the 'other' side Germany

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."
In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

blocks.caption: Waldi entered children's rooms worldwide as an ambassador of a colorful, democratic and friendly West GermanyImage: Wolfgang Maria Weber/picture alliance

blocks.text: A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown, or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs, and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

blocks.caption: The Bremen exhibition is on show until March 28, 2027Image: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The feedback she's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events: "It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

articles.title: Human rights lawyer couple sentenced to 10 years' prison in Pakistan
articles.summary: Imaan Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha were charged over an incident in 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan.

blocks.text: A Pakistani anti-terrorism court has sentenced human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha to 10 years in prison, over an alleged security breach during a cricket tour in 2024.
The couple were accused of removing road barriers and obstructing police officers in Islamabad - charges that both have denied.
Mazari and Chattha were previously sentenced to up to 17 years in prison for social media posts criticising the military.

Pakistan's Supreme Court had suspended those sentences in August, but police re-arrested the couple before they could be released. They have been imprisoned in Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail for the past several months.
This latest case concerns an incident on 25 October 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan.

Prosecutors accused Mazari and Chattha of removing barriers from a road designated for the team's security convoy and obstructing police officers at Zero Point, a major cloverleaf road junction in Islamabad.

They were each sentenced to 10 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Act, as well as additional one-year and two-year terms for obstructing and using force against public servants. All sentences will run concurrently.
The court also fined each of them 200,000 Pakistani Rupees (£541:$723).
In statements recorded during the trial, the couple described themselves as "prisoners of conscience" who had faced state persecution.
"I am being punished for not only supporting my wife's work and activism, but for choosing this path of resisting injustice as our life journey together," Chatta said in his statement to Dawn News.
The couple had earlier said that they were "being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression, and injustice".
Amnesty International has criticised the proceedings, saying the couple were denied an open and fair trial.
"These convictions are an indictment of Pakistan's justice system." said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact.
"Imaan and Hadi are being targeted solely because of their refusal to stop their fearless human rights work and for exercising their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly."
The organisation also raised concerns that the trial had been moved inside the prison, where Mazari and Chattha were kept behind a cage-like structure during hearings.
The couple have faced several criminal cases in recent months.

They have been in custody since 23 January, when they were arrested in a separate case involving an alleged altercation outside the Islamabad High Court. A day later, they were sentenced to up to 17 years in prison under Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act over social media posts critical of the military.

Pakistan's Supreme Court suspended those sentences and granted them bail on 17 September - but they were arrested again the same day in connection with a separate case over a protest in March 2025, in which they were accused of chanting "anti-government slogans" and "blocking roads".
Mazari and Chattha are prominent human rights lawyers who have represented activists, journalists and marginalised communities subjected to enforced disappearances.
Mazari's mother, Shireen Mazari, is a former human rights minister who served in the government of former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan.
The couple's convictions have long drawn criticism from international human rights organisations, which have raised concerns about the treatment of lawyers and activists in Pakistan.

articles.title: PH Army division calls out AI image falsely showing troops' support for Bato dela Rosa
articles.summary: The Philippine Army's 10th Infantry Division (10ID) on Friday warned the public against an AI-generated image circulating on social media that falsely portrays its troops expressing support for…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 3:43pm

Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa tells members of media at the Senate on Wednesday, May 13, 2026, that he will not surrender to the International Criminal Court after it issued an arrest warrant against him in connection with the crimes against humanity case filed against former president Rodrigo Duterte over the extrajudicial killings during his administration. REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez

The Philippine Army's 10th Infantry Division (10ID) on Friday warned the public against an AI-generated image circulating on social media that falsely portrays its troops expressing support for Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa.

"An AI-generated image circulating on social media falsely portrays personnel of the 10th Infantry (Agila) Division, Philippine Army, as expressing political support for Senator Bato dela Rosa," the 10 ID said.
"The manipulated image misrepresents the professionalism and political neutrality of military personnel by fabricating an endorsement that could mislead the public," it added.
Due to this, the 10ID urged the public to verify information through official sources before sharing unverified posts to help prevent the spread of false information and protect the Army's integrity.
The military reiterated its commitment to professionalism and political neutrality, stressing that it serves the Filipino people without political affiliation or preference.

"The Division stands firmly against disinformation and the misuse of artificial intelligence to misrepresent its personnel, emphasizing that its official positions and statements are communicated only through authorized channels," the 10ID said.

Dela Rosa is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in connection with the crimes against humanity case arising from former President Rodrigo Duterte's war on drugs. The senator is accused of being a co-perpetrator in the alleged crimes.

Earlier, the Department of the Interior and Local Government claimed that Dela Rosa was hiding in Mindanao under the protection of an "armed and powerful group," but did not identify the organization. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: 'I made the wrong decision,' Hyrox athlete who soiled herself in race tells BBC
articles.summary: Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Joanna Wietrzyk says her determination to win the Hyrox race in September had clouded her judgement.

blocks.text: Australian Hyrox athlete Joanna Wietrzyk says she made the wrong decision when she continued to race after soiling herself during a competition in Beijing.
Speaking exclusively to the BBC, she suggested her determination to win the race in September had clouded her judgement.
Roughly halfway through her event last month, Wietrzyk suffered a bout of diarrhoea and images of faecal matter on parts of her body were widely shared online.
"I didn't really think about those around me… the decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision and I'm truly sorry for everyone that I did affect," the athlete told the BBC.
She also talked about the effect of the social media reaction after the incident, saying she should not have received "such backlash", and that she is "only human".

articles.title: How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
articles.summary: The alleged scheme used stolen identities to claim US student aid, with Kenyans among those charged.

blocks.text: In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.

Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.

Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid.

US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments, while further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.

At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.

The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.

Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m (£97m) in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.

With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.

In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totaling approximately $1.44m (£1.07m). At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m (£746,445) in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has suspended three Department of Public Works and Highways officials over alleged “ghost” farm-to-market road projects worth P94 million in Davao Occidental.

blocks.text: October 30, 2026 | 3:02pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has suspended three Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials over alleged “ghost” farm-to-market road (FMR) projects worth P94 million in Davao Occidental.
Pending the conclusion of the proceedings, James Ryan Jabonero, Jonathan Relacion and Zesrel Cuga were placed under suspension for no more than six months.
Other respondents could not be suspended because they had already left public service. Five officials were dismissed in June 2026, and one retired in May of the previous year.
Charges of graft and corrupt practices, malversation and falsification of public documents were first filed in May 2026 by Department of Agriculture (DA) Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel.

The DA discovered a pattern among eight FMR projects in which the officials allegedly conspired to submit fabricated Project Status Reports, Statements of Work Accomplished and vouchers to secure state payments for nonexistent infrastructure.
The complaints also named private contractors Allen Borbon of Adan Builders Co. and Marvin Lata Cumbe and Honorio Cumbe of HVC Sagittarius Commercial & Construction.
‘Seasonal issue’
FMR roads help farmers move goods efficiently and may contribute to lower food prices by easing supply issues.
The agriculture department assumed primary control over such projects in early 2026 following investigations into overpriced, incomplete and nonexistent FMRs under the DPWH.

Budget insertions covering infrastructure projects under both agencies, as well as the National Irrigation Administration and the Department of Health, were among the additions to the House’s version of the proposed 2027 national budget flagged by watchdogs and sectoral groups.
The almost P180 billion in funding reportedly came from slashing the budgets of foreign-assisted projects, calamity funds, the EDSA Busway and health programs.

articles.title: Friday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Benjamin Netanyahu has been left without a majority, now it is up to the coalition to find out whether the desire for change will prove to be a defining political…

blocks.text: Good morning. It was described by many Israelis as the most consequential election in their country’s history. And, as the final votes were tallied, it has delivered a result that presents Israel with a significant dilemma.

Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition has lost its mandate while the opposition has a clear majority: but only if the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, led by retired general Gadi Eisenkot, is prepared to make a governing pact with Palestinian Israeli parties, which have secured a historic result.

But the country that is desperate for change remains bitterly divided. After a campaign mired in racism, during which Israel’s far-right demonised the Palestinian population as the enemy within, Netanyahu has gone further since Tuesday’s vote, claiming that Palestinian-led parties have “stolen the election”, despite Israeli authorities insisting there is no evidence of election fraud.
As coalition talks commence, I spoke to our chief Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison in Tel Aviv, about false narratives and the stark choice facing the country. But first, the headlines.
Five big stories
